true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shard' vs 'shards'

`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `shards`. The value is the same comma-joined shard list. Dashboards and queries that slice by shard will not work uniformly across these related flusher metrics. Use the same tag key for all of them.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", resolves through the patched `time` module attribute and does nothing.

The race the comment describes is still present. `join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its loop before it flushes with the new drift. `(msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently.

Use a real sleep captured before patching (e.g. `from time import sleep` as test_flusher.py does), or better, poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher process is never killed because the isinstance check never matches spawn processes

Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `multiprocessing.Process` is `multiprocessing.context.Process`, and `SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of it (both derive from `BaseProcess`). So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and `process.kill()` is never called.

The old code called `kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression. When a process is restarted for the `hang` cause, the hung process keeps running while a replacement is spawned for the same shards. It also shares the same `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values.

If the old process resumes, two flushers work on the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate segments to `buffered-segments`. Each further hang leaks another process, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS.

Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", resolves through the patched `time` module attribute and does nothing.

The race the comment describes is still present. `join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its loop before it flushes with the new drift. `(msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently.

Use a real sleep captured before patching (e.g. `from time import sleep` as test_flusher.py does), or better, poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of loop on deadline, skipping cleanup of remaining processes

When the deadline has passed, the loop does `break`. Every remaining process in `self.processes` is then neither waited on nor terminated.

The previous single-process code always reached the terminate step after the wait. Now, if the first process consumes the timeout, processes 2..N are silently left running. The remaining processes should still be terminated when the deadline is exceeded: skip the wait but not the terminate.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes are capped and the CLI default is 1

The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." The implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes and round-robins shards across them. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option defaults to 1, so production behaviour by default is still a single flusher process handling all shards. Update the docstring to describe the capped, shared-process behaviour.

Redis memory info and stored-segment queries are now repeated per flusher process on the consumer main thread

`submit()` now loops over `self.buffers` and calls `get_memory_info()` and `record_stored_segments()` on each per-process SpansBuffer. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not per shard. With N flusher processes, every submit therefore issues N times the INFO round-trips to every Redis node.

The ratio is unaffected because `used` and `available` are both multiplied by N, so the work is purely redundant. `record_stored_segments()` likewise goes from one pipeline to N.

This cost lands on the consumer main thread, which the PR is trying to keep minimal. Query memory once, for example via the original full-shard buffer, and batch the ZCARDs in a single pipeline.

join() never terminates spawn processes (same isinstance mismatch)

In `join()`, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for `SpawnProcess` objects, so `process.terminate()` is never called. Flusher processes that do not exit before the deadline keep running after the strategy is joined.

On rebalance the consumer process stays alive and builds a new SpanFlusher. Old flusher processes can then keep flushing alongside new ones for the same shards. With N processes per flusher, the number of leaked processes now scales with shard count. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated behavior and passes only by timing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages". It then asserts that no commit happened (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`).

With the implementation, both offsets are marked complete in the worker's `finally`, so a commit of 102 is expected. The assertion only passes because the check runs before the commit thread's 1-second tick fires. On a slow CI run (DB writes for result creation, scheduling) the tick lands inside the window and the test fails.

The test should wait for the commit and assert `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
--max-workers help text is inaccurate

The help text was changed to "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--max-workers` is ignored in `parallel` mode, which uses `--processes`.

In `thread-queue-parallel` it means the number of queues/worker threads, defaulting to 20 when unset. That default is not documented.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function` -> arroyo's `Commit` callable. That callable (`StreamProcessor.__commit`) is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the consumer thread during `submit`/`poll`. It mutates the DLQ buffered-messages state, calls `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` (which checks assignment state) and may call `commit_offsets` synchronously.

Those run concurrently with the main thread's `poll()`, rebalance callbacks and `close()`. During revocation, `close()` sets the event, which wakes the commit thread. The thread then does one more commit while the main thread is inside the revoke callback, so offsets can be staged for partitions being revoked, which raises or races.

Completed offsets should be collected in a thread-safe structure and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

Commit logic requires strictly contiguous offsets; any gap stalls the partition forever

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks at the first offset not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka does not guarantee contiguous offsets for delivered messages: transactional control markers and compacted topics leave gaps.

The same happens for a message whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue`, which `submit` never tracks (the except branch skips it).

A single such gap means the partition never commits again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and a restart reprocesses everything since the gap. The tracker should track the highest contiguous completed offset relative to submitted offsets, e.g. an ordered deque of submitted offsets, rather than assuming offset+1 always exists.

OffsetTracker state is never reset per assignment; revoked partitions poison future commits

The `OffsetTracker` lives on the factory-scoped pool and is never cleared when partitions are revoked. Two failure modes follow on a later assignment:

1. If a revoked partition still has completed-but-uncommitted offsets, the new strategy's commit loop includes that partition in `committable`. Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises for unassigned partitions, so the whole commit fails. Because `mark_committed` is never reached, the same failure repeats every second and no partition ever commits again.
2. Outstanding offsets abandoned at shutdown stay in `outstanding`. If the partition comes back starting at a higher offset, `get_committable_offsets` starts from the stale minimum, hits a permanently outstanding offset and breaks. Commits for that partition stall forever while `all_offsets` grows.

Tracker state should be scoped to the strategy/assignment and pruned on revoke.

Shared queue pool is shut down on strategy close, then reused after rebalance, silently dropping and committing all messages

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates one `FixedQueuePool` and every `create_with_partitions` call (result_consumer.py:254) hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On any partition revocation, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

The next strategy created on reassignment uses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit`'s blanket `except Exception` (lines 317-325) catches it and calls `add_offset` + `complete_offset`.
- The message is therefore treated as successfully processed, and the new commit loop commits past it.

After the first rebalance the uptime consumer stops processing results entirely while still advancing Kafka offsets. This is silent data loss. The pool needs to be owned per strategy, or must not be shut down in `close()`. Enqueue failures must not be marked complete.

Thread-queue tests leak commit threads and run real processors on worker threads against the DB

None of the new `test_thread_queue_parallel*` tests call `close()` on the strategy returned by `create_with_partitions`. Each leaves a daemon commit thread polling every second for the rest of the test run.

`test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` also submits results without mocking the processor. Worker threads then execute real `handle_result` DB/cache queries on separate connections outside the test transaction. They cannot see the test's fixtures, and they leave connections open across tests.

That test also only asserts `queue_pool is None`. It never verifies that queued items were drained or committed.

Unbounded queues with no backpressure, contrary to the docstring

Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring nevertheless claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up".

If `result_processor` slows down (slow DB/cache, one hot subscription clogging a queue), arroyo keeps polling and the consumer reads the backlog into memory without limit. Every message's `WorkItem` (holding the full `Message`) and the `OffsetTracker` sets grow until the process OOMs.

The queues should be bounded, or the total in-flight count capped, raising `MessageRejected` from `submit` when full.

join() ignores timeout, never flushes final commit, and shutdown abandons queued work

`join(timeout)` just calls `close()` again. It ignores the timeout, does not wait for in-flight items, and does not make a final (forced) commit of offsets completed since the last 1-second tick. Every rebalance or shutdown therefore re-delivers up to a second's worth of already-processed results to the next owner.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting the queues, so workers exit after their current item instead of draining, despite the "Gracefully shutdown" docstring.

It then joins each worker sequentially with a 5s timeout. With the default 20 queues and slow processors, a revoke callback can block for up to ~100s, which can exceed the rebalance/poll timeout and get the consumer kicked from the group.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache

The test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" says it sets an allowing permission "to prove this is not checked". It actually stores `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as not granted.

Without the denial cache, the flow would be: cached perms deny, the DB fallback runs, the default `fakeStore` returns no permissions, and the result is deny. So the test passes whether or not the denial cache works.

The value should be `true`, so the cached perms would allow access and only the denial entry can produce `Allowed:false`.

There is also no test that a denial is written to `permDenialCache` after a DB-backed deny, and none for the collision cases above.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous '_' delimiter in denial cache key lets different resources collide

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins userUID, action, name and parent with "_". Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different requests can produce the same key.

Example: dashboard `a_b` in folder `c` and dashboard `a` in folder `b_c` both map to `<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached denial for one makes Check return `Allowed:false` for the other for up to 30s, without ever looking at the user's permissions.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey`, which mixes two value types (bool vs map) in the same key space.

Fix: use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous encoding, such as a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, length-prefixing, or hashing the tuple.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and render identities share denials

The denial key is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent folder. The identity type is not part of it.

Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0", so they get the same denial key. If an anonymous Check on a dashboard is denied, the entry is cached for 30s. A following `render:0` Check for `dashboards:read` on that dashboard then hits the denial cache and is refused, even though the renderer is meant to be granted read on everything. Image rendering breaks for that window.

The reverse also happens. The renderer is denied every non-read action, so a renderer denial can block an anonymous identity whose configured role (e.g. Editor) should allow the action.

Fix: include the identity type in the denial key (and ideally the resolved user UID), or skip the denial cache for render/anonymous.

Every denied check on a new resource now forces a full DB permission fetch

Before this change, a cached permission set answered Check entirely from cache. Now, when the cached set does not allow the request, Check always calls `getIdentityPermissions`. That path no longer consults `permCache` and re-runs the permission store query, plus basic-role and team lookups once those 30s caches expire.

The denial cache only short-circuits repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, folder) tuple. So each distinct resource a user cannot access costs one DB round trip, and singleflight only merges concurrent calls.

For anonymous access (one shared permission set for all anonymous users), requests for many distinct or random dashboard UIDs each trigger a DB query and each add a new denial-cache entry. That is a cheap load-amplification path compared to before.

Possible mitigations: rate-limit or bound the fallback, e.g. only re-query if the cached perms are older than some threshold, or refresh once per user/action rather than per resource.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React key for Grafana rule items in filtered list

The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` received `key={key}`. The replacement `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` inside `rules.map` has no key, although `key` is destructured on the line above for exactly this purpose and the other branches still pass it. React will emit missing-key warnings and fall back to index-based reconciliation for these stateful items, which hold delete-modal and silence-drawer state.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Silence notifications" menu item does nothing in the new list view

The list view now passes only `promRule` to `RuleActionsButtons`, so `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined. `AlertRuleMenu` still shows "Silence notifications" whenever `canSilence` is true, and here that comes from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`. The click handler sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. With no ruler rule, the drawer never opens and the menu item is a dead button. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts the item is present but never clicks it, so this is not caught. The drawer needs to work from the prom rule (UID/labels), or the item should be hidden when it can't be acted on.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause actions silently disappear from the list view

`canDelete`/`canPause` can now be true via the prom-rule abilities. Rendering, however, still requires a ruler rule: `canDelete && rulerRule` here, and `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` for Pause at line 123. The list view no longer loads ruler rules, so users with delete/update permission can no longer delete or pause/resume Grafana rules from the list. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test grants AlertingRuleDelete/Update yet asserts exactly 4 menu items, which locks in this regression. Delete and Pause should work from a GrafanaRuleIdentifier/prom rule (e.g. fetch the ruler rule on demand), or the regression should be made explicit.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the CombinedRule. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false`. Every consumer of `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` loses that guard, including the default (non-V2) RulesTable list and rule details. Edit/Delete/Pause are now offered for Mimir federated rule groups (`source_tenants`). Editing those groups through the Grafana form is not supported and risks rewriting the group without its federation settings. The CombinedRule's group is still available in `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` and should be used to keep the check.

Prom-based abilities exclude Grafana recording rules from Export/Pause/Restore

The ruler-based hook gates ModifyExport/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which covers any Grafana-managed rule including recording rules. The new prom-based hook gates them on `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` instead. In the list view only the prom path is evaluated, so Grafana recording rules lose the "Export" menu entry and the pause ability. The two hooks now disagree for the same rule. Use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` for these actions to keep parity, and keep `alertingRule` only for Silence.

Rule detail link no longer carries returnTo

The removed implementation built the link as `createRelativeUrl('/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view', { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new component drops `returnTo`. Navigating from the list (including a filtered search) to a rule's detail page no longer lets the viewer return to the same list state/filters, which is a UX regression unrelated to removing ruler calls.

Stale doc comment says group is loaded from Ruler endpoint

The JSDoc still says the component "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints", but this PR removes the ruler query and it now only uses the Prometheus endpoint. The comment in `prometheusGroupsGenerator.ts` ("preload ruler rules", variable `cacheAndRulerPreload`) is similarly stale now that the ruler prefetch was removed.

skipToken path grants Duplicate based on Grafana create permission, leaking into data-source rules

When `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gets `skipToken` (rule is undefined), `loading` is false and `isPluginProvided` is false. That makes `duplicateSupported` true, so Duplicate becomes `[true, ctx.hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)]`. `AlertRuleMenu` ORs this with the ruler abilities. For any data-source (cloud) rule, which always takes the skipToken path, "Duplicate" is therefore shown whenever the user has the Grafana rule-create permission. This happens even when the ruler-based check says it is unsupported (ruler unavailable/loading) or not allowed (no external write permission). This affects the existing RulesTable and rule viewer, not just the new list. A skipped rule should return NotSupported for every action. RulesTable tests mock the prom hook to `[false,false]` for cloud rules, which hides this.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Ad-hoc filters and template variables are applied repeatedly to the same query

`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. The sub-requests it builds keep `request.filters` and are passed to `datasource.runQuery`, which goes through `DataSourceWithBackend.query` and calls `applyTemplateVariables(q, scopedVars, request.filters)` again. On the sharding path it happens a third time: `runShardSplitQuery` also applies the variables and filters, then forwards the request, filters included, into `runSplitQuery`.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` adds ad-hoc filters to the expression. Filters added to the stream selector are de-duplicated. For queries with a parser or label filter, though, `addFilterAsLabelFilter` appends a new `| key=`value`` stage on every pass, with no de-duplication. For example, `{app="x"} | json` with ad-hoc filter `level=error` becomes `{app="x"} | json | level=`error` | level=`error`` (three copies on the shard path). The queries sent and shown in the inspector are bloated, and they differ from what the non-split path produces.

Re-running `templateSrv.replace` on already-interpolated text can also re-expand `$name` sequences that came from variable values. The updated shard test expecting `applyTemplateVariables` to be called 5 times encodes this redundant work.

Interpolate once and strip `filters` (or otherwise mark the request as already interpolated) on the sub-requests passed down to `runSplitQuery` and `runQuery`.

Empty-expr filter now runs before interpolation; a variable that resolves to empty can leave the panel loading forever

`runShardSplitQuery` used to interpolate first (`interpolateVariablesInQueries`) and then drop queries with an empty `expr`. The PR reverses this: `.filter((query) => query.expr)` checks the raw expression and only then calls `applyTemplateVariables`.

A target such as `$query`, where the variable resolves to an empty string, now passes the filter and becomes `expr: ''`. The failure path:
- `requestSupportsSharding([query])` is false for an empty expr, so the query lands in the non-shard `otherQueries` group.
- `runSplitQuery` is called for that group and filters it out, because its `expr` is now empty.
- `runSplitGroupedQueries` receives an empty `requests` array. There `requests.filter(...)[0].partition` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`.
- The throw happens synchronously inside the `groupTargetsByQueryType(...).then(...)` callback. It becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the returned Observable never emits or completes.

Result: any panel mixing a shardable query with a query whose variable resolves to empty hangs in the loading state. Filter on `expr` after interpolating, in both `runShardSplitQuery` and `runSplitQuery`, so empty interpolated queries are dropped. Consider also guarding `runSplitGroupedQueries` against an empty `requests` array.

New interpolation test does not cover the behaviour the fix targets and relies on unrealistic `$__auto` replacement

The test only checks that the targets passed to the mocked `runQuery` are interpolated. In production, `runQuery` (via `DataSourceWithBackend.query`) already interpolated targets before this change. So the assertion does not exercise what the PR actually fixes: `calculateStep`, `isLogsQuery` and `querySupportsSplitting` now see interpolated values, e.g. a `$step` variable changing the step-aligned partition boundaries.

The mock `replace` also rewrites `$__auto` to `5m` unconditionally. The real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto` from scopedVars so the backend interpolates it, so the test asserts frontend behaviour that never happens. The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`.

Assert on the computed ranges or grouping for an interpolated `step` instead, and use a regular dashboard variable in place of `$__auto`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a new empty logger, so logged calls cannot be asserted

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a fresh instance, not the receiver. `LoggerMiddleware` now always logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`.

A test that injects a `TestLogger` and checks `InfoLogs.Calls`, `Message` or `Ctx` will therefore always see zero calls. The fake cannot be used to verify the middleware's logging. Returning `f`, or a logger that shares the recorded state, would make the fake usable for this purpose.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running before it

`logRequest` used to add `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `traceID` to the "Plugin Request Completed" (`grafana-data-egress`) log line itself. It now relies entirely on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` and on attributes that `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` placed in the context earlier in the chain.

If `NewLoggerMiddleware` is used without `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` ahead of it, those identifying fields disappear from the egress log with no error. That includes tests, enterprise or other compositions, and any future reordering of `CreateMiddlewares`.

The old doc note saying the instrumentation middleware must sit at the top of the stack was removed, and no replacement documents the new ordering requirement. Either document the requirement on `NewLoggerMiddleware`/`CreateMiddlewares`, or keep the explicit fields in the logger middleware.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and changed log composition are untested

The PR adds a new middleware and moves the source of the egress log's identifying fields (pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, traceID) from explicit parameters to context-derived attributes.

No test checks either of these:
- that `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` attaches the expected attributes for each endpoint;
- that the "Plugin Request Completed" log still carries them when the middlewares are chained in production order.

A regression here, such as a reordering or a missing attribute, would silently degrade the data-egress logs.

Single MetricsMiddleware instance has its `next` field overwritten on every request (data race)

`NewMetricsMiddleware` creates one `*MetricsMiddleware` up front. The returned `ClientMiddlewareFunc` then sets `imw.next = next` and returns that same shared instance.

`client.Decorator` rebuilds the middleware chain on every QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics call through `clientFromMiddlewares`. So concurrent plugin requests write `imw.next` at the same time other goroutines read it via `m.next.QueryData(...)` and similar calls. That is a data race the race detector will flag, and request A may end up running request B's downstream chain.

This pattern was carried over unchanged from `NewInstrumentationMiddleware`. Since this code is being reworked anyway, the middleware should return a fresh struct per call instead, e.g. `&MetricsMiddleware{pluginMetrics: imw.pluginMetrics, pluginRegistry: imw.pluginRegistry, next: next}`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic count-then-insert lets the device limit be exceeded

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then, in a separate statement with no transaction or lock, runs the upsert. Concurrent requests from new devices, within one instance or across HA replicas, can all see `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The stored device count can end up well above the configured limit. The check and the insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with a count guard, or a transaction with appropriate locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected==0 is treated as limit reached, but MySQL reports 0 for unchanged rows

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. With the default go-sql-driver/mysql settings (no clientFoundRows), MySQL counts only rows whose values actually changed. `updated_at` is a second-precision DATETIME, so an update with the same IP, user agent and second (for example, the same device tagged by two HA instances, whose local caches are separate) reports 0 rows. An already-registered device is then rejected as over the limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device is cached before the limit check, so a rejected device is let in on its next request

`tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and it caches whether or not the call succeeds. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request is rejected in `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The device ID is now in the local cache, though, so every following request within the 29-minute TTL returns nil early from `tagDeviceUI` and authenticates. The limit therefore blocks only one request per device per cache period (per instance) and does not really enforce anything. The cache entry should be set only after a successful create/update, or the rejection should be cached and checked.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit is bypassed by omitting the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header

`TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing. It also returns nil when the remote IP cannot be parsed. In both cases `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds without any limit check. The header is fully client-controlled, so any client that leaves it out (curl, scripts, or a modified frontend) gets anonymous access no matter how many devices are already registered. Only cooperating UI clients are affected by the limit. If the limit is meant as an access control, requests without a device ID need a defined policy, such as rejecting them once the limit is enabled and reached.

Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path for all deployments, adding a COUNT(*) per new device

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` with the request context for every deployment, including the default `device_limit = 0`. On each local-cache miss the request waits for a DB upsert. When a limit is set, it also waits for a `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE updated_at BETWEEN` over the whole anon_device table. The cache key is the client-supplied device ID, so a client sending random IDs forces these queries on every request and adds DB load and latency to anonymous auth. Consider keeping the async path when no limit is configured, and caching the device count instead of counting per request.

Limit test does not cover updating an existing device at the limit or the auth-level behavior

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second, new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It does not check the main intended behavior: an already-registered device must still be able to update when the limit is reached. No test covers `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejecting a device over the limit, or repeated requests from a rejected device. Such a test would have caught the local-cache bypass in `tagDeviceUI`.

New `device_limit` setting not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documentation

The new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` key is read here, but `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` and the configuration docs are not updated. Operators have no way to discover the option, or to learn that 0 means unlimited and that devices over the limit lose anonymous access.

ProvideAnonDBStore now requires an int64, which breaks wire injection of anonstore.AnonStore

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` used to receive `anonstore.AnonStore` through dependency injection, which implies `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` is registered as a wire provider (in `pkg/server/wire.go`). The provider signature is now `ProvideAnonDBStore(db.DB, int64)`. Wire cannot resolve a bare `int64`, so code generation fails if the provider is still registered. Any other consumer that injects `anonstore.AnonStore` also loses its provider, or gets a separately constructed store without the limit. wire.go is not part of this change and needs updating, or the limit should come from `*setting.Cfg`.

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` infers type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig

With strictNullChecks, a class field initialized to `undefined` without a type annotation gets the type `undefined`. Code using `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` (typed as `GrafanaBootConfig`) therefore cannot treat it as a number; for example, `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` is a type error. The backend always sends an int64 (0 by default), never undefined. The field should be annotated, e.g. `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined`, or simply default to 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping full ID lists every batch

Every batch in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) logs via `r.log.Error`. This happens even on the normal path, including the final empty batch where count is 0.

The log lines include the full `ids` slice, which can be up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries (tens of thousands in the new test). They also include an `err` field that is always nil at lines 534/554/576.

In production this produces many spurious ERROR entries on every cleanup cycle, multiplied by the new 1-minute ticker. That pollutes logs, can trigger error-based alerting, and can create very large log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The interval for all background cleanup jobs drops from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This covers temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs and query history, not only annotations. The PR description does not mention this, and it looks like a debugging leftover.

`clean()` still uses a 9-minute timeout, which was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval. With a 1-minute ticker, a slow run is followed almost immediately by the next one, so cleanup can run nearly continuously.

There is no server lock around `clean()`, so every replica in an HA setup now hits the database 10x more often. This adds load and contention on exactly the tables (annotation) where the PR is trying to reduce deadlocks. It should be reverted to 10 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Bound-parameter DELETE breaks on MySQL/Postgres for very large batch sizes

The old implementation used a subquery with no bind parameters. The new code binds one `?` per ID for every database except SQLite-with-large-batch.

MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL both cap a statement at 65535 bind parameters. A user who has configured `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` above that will now get an error on every cleanup run, and annotations will never be cleaned.

The parameter-limit workaround only covers SQLite. Either chunk `ids` into sub-batches below each dialect's limit, or apply the inlining approach (the IDs are trusted int64s read from the DB) for all dialects when the batch is large.

Per-subtest cleanup registered after data creation and assertions

`t.Cleanup` that empties `annotation`/`annotation_tag` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and two `require`-based count assertions. All subtests share one DB.

If insertion or either count assertion fails, `FailNow` aborts the subtest before the cleanup is registered. The leftover rows then make every later subtest fail its initial count assertion, which hides the original failure.

The cleanup should be registered before inserting the data.

Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite

`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside the loop allocates and copies the whole accumulated string on every iteration, so the total work is O(n²) in the number of IDs.

This branch only runs when the batch size is above 999, which is exactly the large-batch case. At the batch size of 32767 used in the new test, this amounts to gigabytes of allocation and copying per batch, repeated for every batch until cleanup is done.

Use a `strings.Builder` or `strconv.AppendInt` into a `[]byte` instead, as `getAccessControlFilter` already does in this file.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the base logger in context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` attaches the base logger rather than the `log` built on the previous line, which carries the name, kind and method values. Every other method uses `log`. Logs emitted by downstream storage code during Delete lose the object name and method context.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric

Inside the background goroutine, the legacy `DeleteCollection` result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Legacy delete-collection timings and failures are therefore counted as unified-storage observations, which skews both series.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object name used as the `kind` metric label (unbounded cardinality)

The success path of Delete calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. It passes the resource `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

This mislabels the metric. Worse, it creates a new Prometheus time series for every distinct object name deleted, which is unbounded label cardinality and can blow up memory in Grafana and in the metrics backend. Use `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context and get cancelled when the request returns

Each background goroutine (Create here, and likewise Delete at 110, Update at 135 and DeleteCollection at 163) wraps the incoming request `ctx` with `context.WithTimeoutCause`. The apiserver/net/http cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which happens right after the goroutine is spawned.

As a result, the legacy SQL write will very often fail with `context canceled` before or while it runs. The 10s timeout never applies. The "safe measure" legacy copy silently goes stale, and the only trace is a metric, because the error is not logged.

Fix: use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent. That keeps request-scoped values such as identity and the logger, but drops the cancellation.

Delete no longer removes legacy copy when the object is missing in unified storage

The old implementation treated `NotFound` from unified storage as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. Now any storage error, including NotFound, returns early and skips the legacy delete.

Objects that exist only in legacy, such as ones never migrated or ones whose async create to unified storage was lost, can no longer be removed through the API. They remain as stale data in legacy.

Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries

The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which already exists on the line directly above it in the same hunk. It also pulls in unrelated older otel and plugin-sdk sums that have nothing to do with the dual writer change. This looks like accidental local tooling churn and should be reverted or regenerated cleanly.

Legacy Update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object persisted in unified storage

The previous code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so legacy received exactly the object stored in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`.

That makes legacy compute its own result via `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)`. For patches, the patch is applied against the legacy copy, which may differ from storage. For PUTs, the object carries unified-storage resourceVersion and preconditions, which legacy may reject.

The two stores can therefore silently diverge, or legacy updates can fail. It also reuses a request-scoped objInfo after the request has completed. Restore the wrapper so legacy receives `res`.

Legacy write errors are no longer logged

The previous implementation logged failures from the legacy store. In the new goroutines (Create here, and also Delete, Update and DeleteCollection), the legacy error is used only as a boolean for the duration metric and then discarded.

There is no log entry with the object name or kind or the error cause. Divergence between unified and legacy storage, including the context-cancellation failures, cannot be diagnosed. Log the error inside each goroutine.

Mode 3 unit tests never verify the legacy write happens

Legacy and unified storage share one mock, and the legacy calls run in untracked goroutines that may execute after the test returns. None of the Mode3 tests assert that the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection was invoked, or with which arguments.

The core new behavior, asynchronous propagation to legacy, is untested. That is why bugs like the cancelled-context issue and the wrong metric calls go unnoticed.

The failure case also configures the error via `setupLegacyFn` even though it is named "unified store fails", so the test only passes because the mock is shared. Consider separate mocks and a synchronization point, for example `assert.Eventually` on `AssertCalled`.

Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage create failures are therefore reported as legacy failures, and the storage error metric never sees them. Dashboards and alerts on dual-writer health will be wrong.

Storage Update failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage update errors are therefore attributed to legacy storage in the metrics.

Unordered fire-and-forget legacy writes can apply out of order and leave legacy inconsistent

Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy store, with no ordering, serialization or retry.

A create quickly followed by an update or delete of the same object (as the integration tests do) can reach legacy in any order. For example, the legacy Delete goroutine may run before the legacy Create goroutine. That leaves an orphaned row in legacy that is never cleaned up. An Update can likewise run before the Create and fail.

Since mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback for rolling back modes, this silently corrupts the fallback data. A per-object ordering mechanism, or at least logging and reconciliation, is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache not re-checked after taking the write lock

`GetWebAssets` checks the cache under `RLock`, releases it, then takes the exclusive `Lock`. Once it holds the exclusive lock it never checks again whether another goroutine has already filled `entryPointAssetsCache`.

Outside dev mode, many requests can arrive while the cache is still nil (cold start, or after a failed load that cached nil). All of them queue on the write lock. Each one then re-opens and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` (or would re-fetch from the CDN), one after another, instead of using the value the first holder just stored.

The standard double-checked pattern fixes this: after `Lock()`, do `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Alternatively, use `sync.Once` for the non-dev path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for the data race being fixed

The PR fixes a data race on the package-level `entryPointAssetsCache`, but adds no test that would catch it coming back. A small test that calls `GetWebAssets` from several goroutines against a temp `StaticRootPath` containing a valid `build/assets-manifest.json`, run under `go test -race`, would verify the fix and guard against regressions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions reads the feature flag but always returns false

The function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, so the variable named `enabled` actually means the flag is disabled. Both branches then return `false`.

The flag lookup is dead logic, and the function name, variable name and control flow all suggest the feature can be enabled by the toggle when it cannot. That misleads future maintainers and anyone debugging why enabling `sqlExpressions` has no effect.

Replace it with an explicit hard-disable plus a comment referencing the CVE, or make the intended re-enable condition explicit and correct.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing DuckDB-backed tests for TablesList/NewSQLCommand will now fail

`TablesList` now calls the stub `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands`, which always returns "not implemented". `NewSQLCommand` then always fails with `sql-invalid-sql`.

The existing unit tests in `pkg/expr/sql` (parser tests) and `pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go` call `TablesList`/`NewSQLCommand` with real SQL and assert on the returned table names. This PR does not update, skip or remove them, so they will fail and break CI.

They should be skipped or rewritten to assert the new disabled behaviour.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading and inconsistent errors when SQL expressions are used

On the reader path the user gets "sqlExpressions is not implemented". That is inaccurate: the feature exists but has been deliberately disabled for security.

On the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path (used when the expression parser toggle is off), the request fails inside `TablesList`. The user gets a BadRequest "error reading SQL command", which implies their SQL is invalid. Each attempt also logs at Error level in `parser.go` (and Warn in `sql_command.go`), including the raw user SQL.

Users who enabled the `sqlExpressions` flag get confusing feedback, and logs get noisy. Return a single clear "SQL expressions are disabled" error from both paths, ideally before calling `TablesList`.

No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected on both code paths

This is the in-repo fix for CVE-2024-9264, but no test asserts that SQL expressions are refused.

There are two entry points:
- `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` (the new gate at line 129).
- The legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` path. It does not go through the reader gate and is protected only by the stub DB.

Without tests for both, someone could later restore a real DB implementation or change `enableSqlExpressions`, and nothing would fail to flag the reintroduced RCE/LFI. Add tests that a `type: sql` query fails in `ReadQuery`, and that `NewSQLCommand`/`Execute` cannot run SQL.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Narrowing the lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index key

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole build, and `GetIndex` (RLock) blocked until a build finished, so callers rarely built the same key twice. Now the lock covers only the final map assignment.

`getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized check-then-build. Concurrent `Search` requests and `handleEvent` calls for a namespace not indexed at startup can therefore each run a full build for the same key. Consequences:
- Wasted work.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics incremented multiple times.
- For file-based indexes, the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` fails because the path already exists.
- The last build overwrites the cache entry, so documents that `handleEvent` wrote into an earlier, now-discarded index instance are lost.

A per-key lock or singleflight around build would give the speedup without these races.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs ranges over the index cache without a lock while the watch goroutine can write to it

`TotalDocs` iterates `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to it in `searchSupport.init` (search.go:216), and that call happens after the event-handling goroutine has already started (search.go:207).

That goroutine runs `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache[key] = idx`. A write event for a resource not indexed at startup can therefore mutate the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. Go treats concurrent map iteration plus write as a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error, so the process crashes at startup.

Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`, or compute the total before starting the watch goroutine.

false_positives.candidate:
Data races on shared counters/err in parallel init workers

Inside the `errgroup` workers, two shared variables are written from multiple goroutines without synchronization:
- `totalBatchesIndexed++`
- `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, which writes the outer `err`

Before this PR the global `BuildIndex` lock serialized most of each worker's run. Now that the lock is removed so that builds run in parallel, these races are much more likely to be hit. The reported `namespaced_indexed` span attribute can be wrong, and the race detector will flag the code.

Use a local `err` in the closure and an `atomic.Int64` (or count after `Wait`).

Init failure in constructor leaks the context and background goroutines

When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`.

If `search.init` succeeded but a later step such as `initWatcher` failed, the search watch goroutine and the backend poller started by `WatchWriteEvents` keep running with no owner that can stop them. The search watch uses `context.Background()`.

Call `cancel()` on the error path. Ideally also tear down anything that `search.init` started.

Integration test disabled for postgres instead of being fixed

The PR skips `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` on postgres with the note "works locally". This PR changes startup behaviour: `NewResourceServer` now runs DB init, search index build and watcher setup synchronously.

The skip likely hides a regression or timing problem introduced by that change. For example, the test only sleeps 500ms before probing the HTTP server, and startup now blocks on indexing.

The postgres storage-server startup path loses CI coverage exactly when its behaviour changes.

Stopped server no longer rejects requests

`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". The only way that error reached callers was through the `s.Init(ctx)` check at the top of every gRPC handler, and this PR removes all of those checks.

After `Stop` cancels the server context and stops the backend, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`Read`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search`/blob/health calls will still run against the stopped backend instead of failing fast with a clear error. `initErr` is now effectively dead state outside of `Init`.

Keep a cheap check of a stopped flag (ideally atomic) in the handlers, or remove the misleading `Stop` bookkeeping.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` registers a cleanup for an IDP whose alias is literally "alias". It does not target the `idp-alias-N` providers created in the loop, and line 425 repeats the same mistake for `idp-alias-20`. None of the created IDPs are cleaned up by these registrations, and the cleanup targets a non-existent resource. The cleanup should use the actual alias, e.g. `get("idp-alias-" + i)`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update uses the org-aware wrapped model, so changes to IDPs of disabled orgs are missed

In `update()`, `idpById` comes from `getById()`, which returns the model wrapped by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The cached login lists, however, are built from `idpDelegate.getForLogin`, which only checks the IDP's own `enabled` column. So IDPs of a disabled org are in the cached sets; this is why the bean now re-checks `isEnabled()`.

Scenario: org A is disabled and has a public, enabled IDP X that sits in the `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` login cache. An admin sets X's `BROKER_PUBLIC` to false (or `hideOnLogin` / `linkOnly` to true). `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false because of the wrapper, and `test(updated)` is also false, so the early return at line 405 skips invalidation. When org A is re-enabled, which does not touch the login keys, the stale cached set still contains X. `getById` returns a fresh model whose `isEnabled()` is now true, and the bean only re-checks `isEnabled()`. A private, hidden or link-only broker is then shown on the login page until something else invalidates the cache.

Fix: evaluate the predicate against the raw stored model, e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)` or the unwrapped cached model, as `remove()` already does with `idpDelegate.getByAlias`.

Single cache entry per FetchMode shared across all organizations causes churn and unbounded growth

`cacheKeyForLogin` keys only on realm and mode, while `organizationId` is stored as a searchKey inside one `IdentityProviderListQuery`. Every first login lookup for a not-yet-seen organization invalidates and rebuilds the whole entry for that mode, merging in all previous orgs' sets. In realms with many organizations, this causes repeated invalidation of the shared entry. Concurrent lookups for different orgs race and drop each other's results. The entry also grows roughly as (#orgs × #realm-level login IDPs) for `ALL` mode. Including the organization id in the cache key would avoid both problems.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover encoder calls whose results are discarded

`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` (lines 114-115) build encoders and throw them away. They are re-created inside the `writeDerSeq` call just below.

This is dead code that does extra allocation and encoding on every signature verification, and it makes readers wonder whether something was meant to use those results. Remove both lines.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common without a default implementation. Any `CryptoProvider` implemented outside this repository stops compiling, or fails at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` calls `order()` while sorting. This includes custom providers and implementations in keycloak-client or other downstream projects built against a newer keycloak-common.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep compatibility and still let the bundled providers override it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so real curve sizes and long-form DER lengths are never tested

The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256. The same 32-byte r/s values are reused for ES384 and ES512; they are only zero-padded to 48/66 bytes.

As a result:
- P-384 and P-521 signatures are never exercised.
- A P-521 DER signature is about 139 bytes. That is the only case that triggers the long-form length (>127) path in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength`, and it stays untested.

The test also only checks that the custom encoder and decoder agree with each other. It never compares `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` output with the JDK-produced DER (`sign`), and never checks that the result passes `Signature.verify`. Symmetric bugs in the hand-written ASN.1 code would therefore go unnoticed.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with `secp256r1`/`secp384r1`/`secp521r1` per algorithm, and assert `Arrays.equals(asn1Des, sign)` or verify the re-encoded signature.

Multiple-provider guard removed; equal-order providers are now picked silently by classpath order

`detectProvider` used to throw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. That check protected against a misconfigured classpath, for example one containing both `keycloak-crypto-default` and `keycloak-crypto-fips1402`.

Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, and the sort is stable, so a tie between them is broken by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The other providers are reported only at DEBUG level.

Consequences:
- A FIPS deployment that accidentally has the default provider on the classpath can silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider instead of failing fast.
- `ServiceLoader` instantiates every provider before sorting. The ignored providers' constructors still run their global side effects: FIPS inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at JVM security-provider positions 1-3 and rewrites `ssl.*ManagerFactory.algorithm`, and Default registers BC. The JVM can end up in a mixed state.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least log at WARN) when two or more providers share the highest order. Only allow silent fallback when the winner has a strictly higher order, such as 200 vs the authz-client's 100.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal listener now does no cleanup under V2 (or when FGAP v1 is disabled)

The whole listener is now gated on `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (v1). This was needed because `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws.

As a result, when V2 is enabled, deleting a client leaves behind its per-client resource (named by the client UUID) and any scope permissions referencing it in the admin-permissions resource server. No V2 cleanup was added.

Also, previously the v1 cleanup ran unconditionally. Realms that once used v1 and later disabled the feature will now accumulate orphaned v1 resources and policies for deleted clients, roles and groups.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns "Clients" instead of client IDs and misses per-client resources

`getClientsWithPermission` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` and adds `resource.getName()`.

Per-client resources created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never get a type. They are made with `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner)` and no `setType`. Only the all-clients resource from `init()` has type `Clients`.

As a result:
- Individual client permissions are never found.
- When the all-clients permission is granted, the returned set contains the literal string "Clients" rather than any client id.

Any caller that treats the result as a set of client IDs gets wrong data. Either nothing is found, or a bogus id is returned.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the "Clients" type resource is absent

When no per-client resource exists, the code loads the type resource via `getResourceTypeResource(...)` and passes it straight to `getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. Later it calls `resource.getScopes()`. Neither use is null-checked.

`getResourceTypeResource` returns null in several cases:
- `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false, e.g. the realm's admin permissions were disabled while the admin-permissions client still exists.
- The "Clients" resource does not exist. `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` returns early when the admin-permissions client already exists, so realms initialized before this change never get the new "Clients" resource or the new scopes (configure, map-roles-composite, map-roles-client-scope).

In those cases every client access check by a non-manage-clients admin throws a NullPointerException (500), because the store dereferences `resource.getId()`. The method should return false when the type resource is null.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc for void require* methods says they "Return true"

`requireView()` is documented as "Returns {@code true} if canView() returns true", and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line ~101) as "Returns {@code true} if canViewClientScopes() returns true".

Both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. The other `require*` methods in this interface are documented that way. These two docs are wrong.

New client scopes and override semantics are not actually verified

`testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` grants `CONFIGURE` together with `MAP_ROLES` and `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE`. The composite-mapping success may therefore come from configure/manage-role checks rather than the new `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE` scope.

Other gaps:
- No test covers `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`.
- No test covers `getClientsWithPermission`.
- No test covers a per-client NEGATIVE permission combined with an all-clients permission, as is done for users.

These tests would have exposed the canView short-circuit and the getClientsWithPermission bug.

Repeated full policy evaluations per client check

Each `hasPermission(client, scope)` call:
- performs a full policy evaluation over all scopes of the resource, then discards everything but one scope;
- on the fallback path, also runs a `findByResource` query.

`canView(client)` chains `canView()`, then `canConfigure` → `canManage` → `hasPermission(MANAGE)`, then `hasPermission(CONFIGURE)`, then `hasPermission(VIEW)`. That is up to four evaluations of essentially the same resource. `getAccess(client)` repeats this for view, manage and configure.

When listing clients without the view-clients role, this runs for every client in the realm. Evaluate once and check the granted scopes set, or cache per request.

Tests mutate shared realm state without cleanup

Some tests change realm state and never restore it:
- `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles `myclient-role` and `myclient-subRole`, maps one to `myadmin`, and adds a composite. It registers no `realm.cleanup()` actions.
- `testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` and moves a default client scope to optional without reverting.

Other tests in the class index into `getDefaultClientScopes()` and depend on `myclient`'s state. These changes make results order-dependent, and a role-create conflict will occur if the realm is reused.

canView(client) short-circuits on all-clients VIEW, so per-client deny permissions cannot restrict view

`canView(ClientModel)` returns true as soon as `canView()` is true. `canView()` includes `hasPermission(VIEW)`, which evaluates only the all-clients "Clients" resource.

So if an admin is granted VIEW on all clients, a per-client NEGATIVE VIEW permission for a specific client is never consulted. The admin can still view that client.

This contradicts the resource-specific-overrides-type semantics used elsewhere in V2. For users, `testViewUserPermission` shows a per-user deny overriding the all-users allow. Here an administrator cannot hide individual clients from someone holding all-clients VIEW.

`canView(client)` should only short-circuit on the admin roles (`canViewClientDefault`). The VIEW decision should go through `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`, which already falls back to the all-clients resource.

getResourceName not updated for the Clients resource type

`getResourceName` maps only `Users` resources: "All users" for the type resource, or the username for a user. For policies of type `Clients` it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Neither the per-client resources (created with only a name) nor the "Clients" type resource have a display name. Permission representations for client permissions will therefore show null resource names instead of the clientId or an "All clients" label.

Add a `CLIENTS` branch that resolves the client by id and returns its clientId.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Appending `--features=rolling-updates` to every documented command overrides the user's feature configuration

The `updatecompatibility` macro now hard-codes `--features=rolling-updates` on every documented invocation. A CLI option takes precedence over keycloak.conf and env, so any features the user already enables (e.g. `features=token-exchange` in the config file) are replaced for that run. That contradicts the guide's warning that the command must be run with exactly the same configuration as the deployment. A user who also passes their own `--features` gets a duplicate option.

`features` is also a build-time option. With an optimized/pre-built image (`--optimized`, which these commands support via `OptimizedMixin`), a runtime `--features` value is not applied. The check then reads the build-time profile and exits with "feature disabled" unless the image was built with the feature, as the PR itself does in `Dockerfile-custom-image`.

The docs should tell users to add `rolling-updates` to their existing feature list and to include it at build time for optimized images.

Docs say the Operator fails without `rolling-updates`, but nothing enforces it

The new CAUTION says the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or the Operator will fail. This PR adds no Operator validation that inspects the CR's enabled features. The `ROLLING_UPDATES` enum constant is new here, so no earlier check could reference it. The Operator also does not run the `update-compatibility` commands in this version; the only update strategy is Recreate (or unset). So setting `spec.update.strategy: Recreate` without the feature still works, and the documented failure never happens. `UpgradeTest` enables the feature only when a strategy is set and never covers the claimed failure. Either add a reconcile-time validation that reports an error status when `spec.update` is used without the feature, or correct the documentation.
